old: Long before it named a swagger, this idea lived in the sound of someone loudly talking themselves up.
At its root is a French word that simply meant boasting or bragging.
It shares an Italian ancestor with a word for a dazzling, showy display of skill — bravura.
clues: This noun names a kind of outward display of attitude, and it traces back to an Italian verb meaning "to brag, to boast."
It is a loud, swaggering show of confidence or courage, often put on to hide fear. Unlike true bravery, it is mostly performance meant to impress others.
People often call it "false" when it masks nerves, like a boxer's boasts before a fight. It shares its root with bravura, from the same Italian family of boldness and show.
